full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman J: Both the Civil Appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and order dated 4-8-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011 making the Rules Nisi absolute, and declared the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No.83 of 2003 to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 The present respondent No.1 in both the civil appeals as the writ petitioners preferred the Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011 before the High Court Division challenging the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No.83 of 2003 (Anx.5/02) (Ka-43 House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka) allowing the case with direction to exclude the property in House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka from the list of abandoned buildings stating that the land measuring 131 square yards (1 and 3/4 kathas) of House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka was allotted/leased out on 21-10-1963 by Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka as lessor in favour of Noor Mohammad, displaced person from India, and accordingly possession of the said land was handed over to him. After taking over possession of the said land, the said Noor Mohammad had been possessing the same by erecting dwelling house, and started living therein; during Liberation War, the said Noor Mohammad along with his family left the said house and after liberation he did not come back to the said house and, as such, Government took over possession the same as abandoned property. Thereafter, Mr Ataharul Hoque, the writ petitioner of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 entered into possession of the said house on 1-5-1972 and started to live therein with his family. He by dint of possession filed an application to the concerned authority for allotting the said House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka in his favour. On the basis of the said application, the writ respondent No.2 of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 issued a Demand Note on 18-1-1975 upon the applicant with a direction to deposit arrear rent from 1-5-1972 to 31-12-1975 at the rate of Taka 85 per month amounting to Taka 2,720 within 23-1-1975. As per direction of the writ respondent No.2 the writ petitioner deposited the said amount of Taka 2,720 through Challan No.H/47 dated 23-1-1975 as arrear monthly rent of the said house, and on the same date it was duly informed to the Executive Engineer, Housing Settlement, Mirpur Division, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka, and on 29-1-1975, the same was also duly informed to the office of the Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur and Mirpur Housing Estate Area. Subsequently, the writ petitioner on 3-10-1982 deposited an amount of Taka 510/through Bangladesh Bank Chalan No.Uma/10 and on 29-4-1985 also deposited an amount of Taka 13,134.40 through Bangladesh Bank Chalan No.Jha-3/4 as rents for the said abandoned property. In this way the writ petitioner deposited total amount of Taka 16,364.40 as rents of the said house. Since the original allottee of the property in question had been untraceable and the property in question was uncared in 1972, the property was declared by the Government as abandoned property and it took over the possession in the property as abandoned. The writ petitioner of Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 has been possessing the same as tenant under the Government since 1972. The Government included the said abandoned Building in the `Kr' list of the Abandoned Buildings at Serial No.43 published in Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986 at page No.9762 (58). In the meantime, the writ respondent No.2 of Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 vide Memorandum No.শাখা-৭/এপি-৮৫/৮৪/৪৮০ dated 25-3-1985 issued a letter offering to sell the property in favour of the writ petitioner. As per condition Nos.1, 2 and 3 of the said offer letter the writ petitioner on 17-11-1985 deposited the 1st installment of an amount of Taka 23,465.20 as 20% of the total consideration amounting to Taka 1,17,326 and also submitted an affidavit on 29-10-1985 and certificate with regard to full payment of rent of the property in question obtained from appropriate authority. After completion of all formalities a “বিক্রয় চুক্তি” was executed on 9-10-1986 between the writ petitioner and the Government with regard to the property in question. (as described in the schedule below.) On 28-1 1 - 1 9 8 5 the Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 was promulgated and the list of abandoned properties was published on 23-9-1986, and thereafter “বিক্রয় চুক্তি”was executed by the Government in favour of the writ petitioner on 9-10-1986. From the Memo No.569 dated 8-10-1988 the writ petitioner learnt that the original allottee did not deposit the total  consideration amount against the property in question. The writ petitioner learnt that the writ respondent No.4, Md Murtuza Shah filed Case No.83 of 2003 in the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka praying for exclusion of the property from the abandoned properties List. 

 4. The writ petitioner of the instant writ petition in Settlement Case No.83 of 2003 submitted an application which pending before the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka enclosing the above mentioned documents including the Municipality Tax and other utilities bills paid by him in connection with the ownership, occupation and possession of the property in question, as, well as certificate issued by the Local Commissioner for addition of party. But the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka refused to accept the said application filed by the writ petitioner. During the trial of the case before the Settlement Court No.1, Dhaka PWs were examined including the said Mr Md Murtuza Shah as PW 1. There are serious of anomalies and contradictions in the depositions of the witnesses, which will be apparent upon perusal of the depositions. The writ respondent No.4 made some false, malafide and irrelevant statements in the applications while filed the alleged application. 

 5. The First Court of Settlement, Dhaka after hearing the parties, allowed the Case No.83 of 2003 with direction to exclude the property in question from the "Ka" list of the abandoned buildings by the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006. 

 6. Against the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka, the writ petitioners of Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011, finding no other alternative efficacious remedy, moved the above mentioned writ petitions and obtained the Rules Nisi. 

 8. A Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties in both writ petitions made the Rules Nisi absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment of the Settlement Court by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-8-2011. 

 10. Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, the learned Senior Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant in both the civil appeals submits that, the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the respondent No.1 (writ petitioner) being a third party had no locus stanch' to file the writ petition challenging the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He further submits that, the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the Government could not produce any evidence either documentary or oral to show that the property in question comes within the definition of "abandoned property" under Article 2 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He next submits that the High Court Division erred in law having failed to consider that the original allottee late Noor Mohammad (father of the appellants), filed an application to the appropriate authority with proper documents within time stipulated by law to get his property released and the Court of Settlement after meticulous assessment of materials on record passed its judgment excluding the property in question from the 'Ka' list of the Abandoned Buildings as per provision of law enacted under the Ordinance No.54 of 1985 and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He finally submits that the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the explanation of delay in filing the writ petition is not satisfactory and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and the instant appeals should be allowed. 

 11. Per contra, Mr SK Shaifuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016 and the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016 submits that the appellants having miserably failed to discharge the burden to prove that the property in question is not an abandoned property on or before 28-2-1972. Since onus of disproving of abandoned property is squarely lies upon them as provided in section 5 of the Ordinance, No. LIV of 1985 and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He further submits that Mr Ataharul Hague being the Government Demand Note Holder entered into an agreement for sale on 9-10-1986 with the Government as per Sale Offer vide Memorandum No শাখা-৭/এপি-৮৫/৮৪/৪৮০ dated 25-3-1985 and paid 1st installment of Taka 23,465.20 as 20% of the Total consideration and, as such, he had got locus-stanch to file the writ petition before the High Court Division as per section 13 of the State Agreement as “১৩। তফসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কে ভবিষ্যত কোন মামলা-মোকদ্দমার উদ্ভব হইলে ক্রেতা নিজ দায়িত্বে উহা পরিচালনা করিনে।”and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He next submits that, the Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant and even if, any singular failure on the part of the claimants regarding whereabouts of the Original Lessee at the relevant point of date i.e. on 28-2-1972 is fully and wholly stunning and, as such, the High Court Division has rightly made the Rule absolute. Hence, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He finally submits that the Government has got right to property as Lessor and the Government-writ petitioner filed the writ petition with proper explanation of delay although there is no statutory limitation to challenge the legality and propriety of the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement and the High Court Division, having assessed the evidence on record, made the Rules Nisi absolute and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. 

 13. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant in both the civil appeals, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016, the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016, also Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016 and the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, judgment of the Court of Settlement, other connected materials available on record. 

 14. In the instant appeals leave were granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that respondent No.1 (Writ Petitioner) being third party had no locus standi to file the writ petition challenging the judgment and order of the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka allowing the case and directing the Government to exclude the case property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings. 

 16. Thirdly, as to whether the High Court Division erred in law in failing to appreciate that the explanation of delay in filing the writ petition is not satisfactory and the Court of Settlement passed the judgment and order after proper and meticulous assessment of evidence on record allowing the case and directing the Government to exclude the case property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings. 

 17. As regards to the ground filing of writ petition by the third party is required to scan as to whether he has any legal right over the property in question pending settlement case between the admitted allottee owner and Government Lessor. The original allottee when questioning the vesting of properly, as per section 7 of the said ordinance as to the abandoned property and listing the same in "Ka" list, before the competent Settlement Court to decide the propriety of vesting, there is no reason and scope to resolve any claim made by the third party through Government vide a contract of purchase. Because, the provision of ordinance provides no room to resolve any claim of right and title of contracting party by the Court of Settlement. The Court of settlement only can see as per application under section 7 of the ordinance, as to whether the case property is abandoned or not. 

 18. The High Court Division in the judgment has already noticed that the respondent No.1 Ataharul Hague had applied to be added as a party in the settlement case before the Court of Settlement which was refused. The respondent No.1 did not challenge the order of refusal, nevertheless, after passing the judgment by the Settlement Court excluding the property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings filed the writ petition challenging the aforementioned excluding before the High Court Division. In the above facts and circumstances, this Division is of the firmed view that writ petition by the third party could not be maintainable, rather, it is quite superfluous. In this regard we can safely held that before issuing the Rule the High Court Division ought to have gone through the merit of the Writ Petition and if it is apparent from the statement of the Writ Petition that the Petitioner neither aggrieved person nor have any locus standi to file the Writ Petition, such type of Vexatious application should be rejected summarily .The Writ Petitioner of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 has got no personal interest in the case property either as tenant or so called purchaser. His claim must be governed according to the result of his landlord vendor's case. It is, therefore, our considered view that the High Court Division appears to have misconstrued and misconceived their jurisdiction under article 102 in holding that the Writ Petition is maintainable. 

 21. On a careful perusal of the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is clearly revealed that the petitioner before the Court of Settlement produced 10 (ten) prosecution witnesses and exhibited so many documents. 

 22. On the other hand the respondent Government neither produced any oral or documentary evidence for rebutting the prosecution explanation offered in the oral and documentary evidences regarding Noor Mohammod's living in Bangladesh. Rather, from the trend of the cross it reveals that they would like to establish that claimants are not the legal heirs of the late Noor Mohammod. It is must be mentioned here that Noor Mohammod had filed the application on 17-09-1986 under section 7 of the ordinance LIV of 1985, the final gazette was published on 23-9-1986 including the property as abandoned property at page no. 9762 (58) being serial No.43. In respect of the legal heirs, the petitioners before the settlement Court filed the copy of succession certificate vide Succession case No. 631 of 1996, certificate being issued by a competent Court which did not revoke till today. More so, they had deposited some certificate copies of the complaint case being No. 5 of 97 of the tribunal No. 1 of Bangladesh Bar Council and copy of passport of the Noor Mohammod. Noor Mohammod died on 10-2-1987. The leave petitioners were substituted by the settlement Court as the legal heirs. The government did not challenge those events before any court. 

 23. The Settlement Court found from the evidence on record that Noor Mohammod never left Bangladesh, rather, on 4-2-1972 he shifted from the property in question for fear of his life to House No.7, Land No.4, Block-C, Avenuce-3, section 11 of Mirpur, Dhaka. So, there is no question arises as to Noor Mohammod's leaving the country. There is no iota of evidence on the side of the Government that, Noor Mohammod had not shifted the house nor they had produced any oral and documentary evidences that Noor Mohammod left Bangladesh. It is further depicted from the record that Noor Mohammod could not manage or supervise the case property, for a short period. The such type of absence from the case property does not take away his right and title in respect of case property as he did not left the country, rather had been trying to release the property. Therefore, the Court of Settlement rightly found that Noor Mohammod never left Bangladesh. It was also found by the Court of Settlement that Noor Mohammod had applied for passport and on 24-9-1979 a passport was issued in the name of Noor Mohammod as a permanent resident of Bangladesh. This passport proved that Noor Mohammod was a permanent resident of Bangladesh until death and lived in Bangladesh. He died on 10-2-1987 which has been clearly mentioned in a Death Certificate issued by the Local Commissioner and certificate issued from the concerned authority of the graveyard. Therefore, the Court of Settlement believed the prosecution story thoroughly examining the oral deposition and documentary evidence. The High Court Division without controverting the aforesaid unimpeachable evidence, reversed the facts of finding of the Court of Settlement, as if, it is a Court of appeal which is not only beyond the jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution, rather, such exercise is colourable and fenciful which is deprecated by this Division. So, the High Court Division under article 102 could not act as a Court of appeal. 

 24. This Division in the long line of catena has already held that the High Court Division only could interfere with the finding of the Court of Settlement, if could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made findings upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence causing prejudice to a party or it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. The High Court Division has failed to appreciate any such lacking in the judgment of Settlement Court, even then, it set aside the judgment of settlement Court. 

 25. Noor Mohammod had filed the application on 17-9-1986 to the abandoned property cell of Ministry of Works for releasing the property vide a receipt No.3712 which has ultimately given rising to Settlement Case No.83 of 2003. So, it is crystal clear that the Late Noor Mohammad had filed the application within time as per provision of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 though the case Number was recorded in the year 2003. 

 26. It is, therefore, clearly depicted that the filling of case in the Court of Settlement by the Noor Mohammod not barred by law as opined by the High Court Division. It is therefore obvious, the findings in the judgment of High Court Division as to non-consideration of evidence by the Settlement Court bears no significance. Ratherest, the Judgment of the High Court Division is so inappreciable which justifying calls for interference by this Division. 

 27. The next ground is whether the High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that sole respondent of the settlement case Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works filed the writ petition without any delay acting with due diligence. On a careful scrutiny of the record of the Writ Petition No.2516 of 2011 it is apparent on the face of the cause title of the writ petition that the impugned judgment was passed on 3-5-2006, and an affidavit was sworn on 22nd day of March 2011; therefore, filing of the writ petition was not only delayed, ratherest, shockingly and unprecedented delay has been caused in invoking the special original jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution, though settlement case was allowed on contest against the writ petitioner Government denying the material allegations, not only that, moreso, they also cross examined all the PWs.
